chapters.title: The Hour on the Register
chapters.text: Mateo Salvaterra reached the plateau field long after midnight, because the bus from Alendal had broken an axle in the dry hills and its passengers had walked the last stretch by torchlight. By morning the horn on the hangar pole was playing a speech about the country's patience. Gabriel Tenorio was taking a wheel off one aircraft to put it on another and did not stop to shake hands. Noemi Arcos offered Mateo half an orange and the only shade on the apron. In the operations office Sofia Landa turned the arrival register toward him. She had already typed his arrival as eight o'clock on the last evening of the old year, the hour his posting order named and the commander expected to read. 'The carbon keeps whatever we tell it,' she said, and held out a pencil.

options.label: Ask Sofia to type the hour I really arrived.
options.reply: Sofia retypes the page without comment; by noon the commander has asked why his newest pilot cannot keep to a bus timetable.

options.label: Sign the hour the order expected.
options.reply: Sofia pencils the true hour on her carbon alone, and Mateo begins his posting owing her a small, friendly silence.

chapters.title: Two Tyres from Town
chapters.text: Wages were three months late, and the base ran out of tyres before it ran out of speeches. Gabriel solved the second problem first. On the morning Mateo had the duty book, he found Gabriel in the hangar mouth rolling four drums of fuel onto the back of a small bowser. Orozco, who kept a parts yard in town, had two good tyres and no use for promises from Alendal; he would take fuel. 'Write test run,' Gabriel said, 'and by tonight your aircraft will stand on rubber instead of rims.' Noemi, eating breakfast on an upturned crate, read the situation in one glance and chewed slowly enough to hear the answer. Mateo held the pen over the fuel column. He had come to serve something larger than a town yard. He had not expected it to depend on one.

options.label: Write the drums and the trade into the fuel book.
options.reply: Gabriel drives out anyway, shaking his head; the commander will read an honest line by noon and look for somebody to blame.

options.label: Write test run and wave the bowser out.
options.reply: The tyres arrive before dark; Gabriel spikes Orozco's receipt above his bench and begins treating Mateo as one of his own.

chapters.title: The Speech on the Pole
chapters.text: The national day speech came down the horn on the hangar pole from Alendal, and the whole base stood on the apron to receive it. The voice said the north had grown rich on the south's patience, and that patience was not a debt Leasath would owe forever. Mateo had been chosen to read the closing passage from a card; he had copied its best sentence into his pocket notebook the night before. Behind him Noemi murmured that a rich neighbor might at least lend them tyres, and the second rank laughed. Afterwards the adjutant told Sofia to type a list of everyone who had laughed. Sofia rolled a sheet and a carbon into her machine and waited. Mateo stood at her desk still holding the card. He had heard exactly who spoke first.

options.label: Let Noemi put her own name on the list.
options.reply: Noemi signs with a flourish and spends a week on kitchen duty; the second rank stops laughing at anything within her hearing.

options.label: Hand the adjutant a list with no names on it.
options.reply: Sofia types 'no individual identified' and pencils the truth on her carbon; the four share a joke the adjutant will never hear.

chapters.title: Blankets by the Hundred
chapters.text: When the river broke its banks in the lowlands, the plateau field sent everything it could lift. There had been fuel for the lorries or for the aircraft, not both, and the aircraft stayed on the ground. Three days later Sofia stood in Gabriel's stores cage with the commander's draft for the Alendal papers: two thousand blankets, twelve relief flights, the base's finest week. Gabriel's paper tags said four hundred and eleven blankets, most of them stripped from barracks beds, and no flights at all. Noemi was sleeping on a bare mattress and said she did not mind. Mateo minded; he had loaded every bundle and wanted the work counted as it was. The commander had explained, kindly, that large numbers brought money for wages. Sofia held the draft in one hand and the tags in the other.

options.label: Let the commander's figure stand.
options.reply: The money arrives and the barracks get new blankets; Sofia files Gabriel's tags behind the top copy, where only the four know to look.

options.label: Send the count from Gabriel's tags.
options.reply: The papers print a smaller, truer story; the money from Alendal shrinks with it, and the commander stops greeting Sofia in the corridor.

callback.text: Noemi has not forgotten her week of kitchen duty. She says it taught her that a list with real names on it at least tells you who to argue with.

condition_variants.trigger: has_capitulated = no has_war = no ac_sq_air_capable = yes
condition_variants.text: Mateo flew the third relief flight with Noemi in the rear seat counting rooftops. The river had spread into a brown sheet the width of the valley, and the trainer's fuel pump coughed twice over the water, each time long enough for Mateo to choose a field he could not have reached. Noemi talked him through it by describing what lay below: a red roof, a family on it, a goat on the family's shed. They dropped their bundles and turned for home with the pump still muttering. That night Gabriel had it in pieces on the bench when Sofia came into the stores cage with the commander's draft for the Alendal papers: twelve relief flights, two thousand blankets. Gabriel's tags said three flights and four hundred and eleven blankets. Mateo had flown all three.

chapters.title: Oranges at the Gate
chapters.text: The crate came up the hill road on a growers' lorry with Noemi's name painted on the slats in her mother's hand. The corporal at the gate would not release it. A new instruction from Alendal required a permit for parcels from the hill districts, and the permit asked for the sender's address, occupation and associations. Noemi read her mother's letter in the guard hut. The harvest was thin, her mother's knee was worse, and Ruben had joined the growers' association that the radio had begun calling agitators. Gabriel arrived with a few coins in his fist and the air of a man who had settled worse things with less. Sofia had brought the blank permit and a carbon. Mateo could smell the oranges through the slats and found himself wondering who, exactly, the instruction protected.

options.label: File the permit honestly, associations and all.
options.reply: Sofia types Ruben's association into a government form; the crate is released eleven days later, half spoiled, and Noemi thanks her stiffly.

options.label: Let Gabriel settle it with the corporal.
options.reply: A coin and a packet of cigarettes change hands; the four eat oranges on the hangar step, and Gabriel keeps the slats for something useful.

callback.text: Sofia still keeps the smaller flood count on her carbon. The commander has not forgiven it, which makes a second government form feel heavier in her hands.

chapters.title: Names on a Clipboard
chapters.text: Lieutenant Abel Quintana brought the clipboard into the hangar at lunch, when the officers were easiest to find. Its first paragraph asked Alendal to restore the base's pay and to look into where the commander's spare fuel had been going. Its second declared that the undersigned stood ready to end the north's long exploitation of Leasath. Mateo signed below Abel with a hand steadier than he felt. Noemi read both paragraphs, laughed once and handed back the pen. Gabriel, who as a sergeant could not sign, wanted the first paragraph and pretended not to have read the second. Sofia's carbons now lived on a shelf Gabriel had built her from orange-crate slats, and she knew which shelf the commander would ask her to search. That evening the four ate supper without once mentioning the clipboard.

options.label: Tell Noemi why I signed, both paragraphs.
options.reply: They argue on the hangar step past midnight; Noemi does not change Mateo's mind, but she stops having to guess at it.

options.label: Agree that the four of us will not discuss it.
options.reply: Supper becomes easy again, and when the commander asks, none of them will have heard anything worth repeating.

callback.text: Gabriel built the shelf from the crate he once bought past the gate. He likes to say that the wood, at least, was honestly come by.

chapters.title: The Evaluation in Carbon
chapters.text: The petition had gone nowhere, and Abel Quintana had resigned in the spring rather than wait to be moved somewhere worse. The commander stayed. In June he dictated the year's evaluations to Sofia in a single afternoon, and Mateo was made flight lead. Noemi's flying scores were better than his; everybody on the plateau knew it, including Mateo. Her evaluation said so, and then said: attitude unsuitable for leadership. Mateo found the carbon by accident on the slat shelf while looking for a fuel return. Sofia did not pretend he had not seen it. Gabriel, who had come in with a spare part and a cigarette, read the line upside down and swore quietly. Noemi was outside on the apron, walking a cadet through his checks and laughing with him in a way the commander would have recorded.

options.label: Show Noemi the carbon of her evaluation.
options.reply: Noemi reads the line twice, then congratulates Mateo properly; it is worse than shouting would have been, and more honest.

options.label: Take the promotion and look after Noemi quietly.
options.reply: Mateo arranges her the better aircraft and the kinder schedules, a private kindness she accepts without knowing what it repays.

options.label: Ask the commander, in writing, to correct it.
options.reply: The commander lets the promotion and the evaluation both stand, in writing; Sofia files his refusal beside the line, and Noemi hears of it from Gabriel.

callback.text: Mateo and Noemi once argued about the petition until midnight. The habit makes it harder for him to pretend he cannot guess what she would want now.

chapters.title: The Valve from Orozco's Yard
chapters.text: The valve failed on a ground run with Noemi in the cockpit, and she had the engine shut down before the smell reached the hangar door. Nobody was hurt. In the stores cage, under the bench lamp, Gabriel showed the others the casting: a copy, good enough to pass a glance, from a crate he had bought at Orozco's yard. His paper tag still hung from it. He had written the truth in the aircraft's own logbook, because an airframe's book was the one thing he had never bent. The stores book said the valve had come from the depot in Alendal. Next week an inspector was coming to ask about copied valves after a crash at another field. Orozco also kept the town hospital's generators running. Mateo asked what was in the rest of the crate. Sofia asked which book the inspector would be shown.

options.label: Send the copies back to Orozco and show the stores book.
options.reply: Gabriel drives the remaining valves back to town himself, and the inspector reads a stores book that agrees with itself and nobody else.

options.label: Show the inspector the tag and Orozco's name.
options.reply: Gabriel loses a supplier and gains a reprimand; the inspector leaves with a lead, and the hospital is left with a problem.

callback.text: Gabriel's spike still holds Orozco's receipt for the two tyres Mateo once kept out of the fuel book. Mateo recognizes the handwriting on the new tag.

chapters.title: A Visitor without a Purpose
chapters.text: Ruben Arcos came to the gate on a borrowed motorcycle, thinner than his photograph and very pleased to see his sister. Mateo had the visitor register that afternoon. A standing order required every visitor from the hill districts to give a name and a purpose, and the corporal had underlined purpose twice. Ruben had been held for a night after a growers' meeting the year before. He asked, politely, whether 'family' would do. Noemi stood behind him with her arms folded and gave Mateo nothing to read in her face. In fifteen years she had never asked him for anything at a gate. Gabriel, passing with a trolley of tyres, slowed to listen. Sofia would type the register into the weekly return on Monday, and the return went to Alendal. Mateo uncapped the pen.

options.label: Write his full name and the purpose he gives.
options.reply: Ruben writes 'to see my sister' in his own hand; Noemi says nothing about it for a month, then thanks Mateo for not lying.

options.label: Write 'family visitor' and leave his name off.
options.reply: Ruben and Noemi walk the fence for an hour; Monday's return is one name shorter, and Mateo carries a secret he did not ask for.

options.label: Hand Noemi the pen and let her write it.
options.reply: She writes her brother's name and 'family'; the entry is true and incomplete, and for once the choice of what to leave out is hers.

callback.text: Noemi still keeps the carbon of her evaluation folded in her flight jacket. Mateo knows she will judge this entry by the same standard.

chapters.title: The Speech Mateo Was Given
chapters.text: The night before the anniversary visit, the four climbed onto the barracks roof with Sofia's draft and two bottles of beer Gabriel had obtained without explanation. Mateo was to address the cadets in front of the minister. The commander had added three sentences to Sofia's text: that the north had fed on Leasath for a generation, that the country's patience was ending, and that young pilots should be ready to collect what was owed. Mateo read them aloud to the dark plateau. They sounded like the sentences in his notebook, the ones he had been copying since his first year, and he could no longer tell whether that made them his. Noemi lay on her back counting satellites. Sofia said she had written the other paragraphs, and would like to hear which ones he kept.

options.label: Give the speech without the commander's sentences.
options.reply: The cadets hear a shorter speech about care and craft; the commander hears exactly what is missing, and so does the minister's aide.

options.label: Read the draft as written, every line.
options.reply: The cadets applaud on cue and the commander shakes Mateo's hand; afterwards, on the roof, Noemi asks which lines were his.

callback.text: They once agreed not to discuss the petition. The silence has kept supper pleasant for eight years, and it means nobody on the roof knows what Mateo believes.

chapters.title: The Register of Home Districts
chapters.text: In June the commander ordered a register of every person's home district and next of kin, for travel passes, he said, though nobody on the plateau could remember needing one. The gate now closed at dusk. Sofia set up a folding table beside the guard hut with a duplicate book and its carbon, and took names as people came off shift, so that nobody could forget to be counted. Noemi's district was in the hill country, and her brother's name had been on the wrong sort of list since the growers' meetings. Mateo, a flight lead with a desk of his own now, told her to give everything at once, before somebody else did it for her. He meant it as protection. Gabriel asked whose protection, and nobody answered. Noemi stood at the table and read the line headed relatives.

options.label: Put Noemi's family on the register in full.
options.reply: Noemi gives her mother's street and Ruben's name; within a month she is grounded for a review that takes the rest of the year.

options.label: List her district and leave her brother off.
options.reply: Sofia writes a smaller family than Noemi has; Noemi keeps flying, and the four now share a gap in an official register.

callback.text: Ruben's own handwriting already sits in the gate register from his visit. Sofia points out that the base has, in a sense, been told before.

condition_variants.text: By June the country had two hands, and each claimed to be the one giving orders. The hill districts had gone over to the other side in the spring, the road beyond the plateau was closed at the river, and the horn on the hangar pole read out emergency decrees between the weather reports. Then the commander ordered a register of everyone with family across the line. Sofia set up a folding table beside the guard hut with a duplicate book and its carbon, and took names as people came off shift. Noemi's mother lived four streets from her town's square, and Ruben had been on lists of a different kind since the growers' meetings. Mateo told Noemi to give everything at once, before somebody else did it for her. He meant it as protection. Gabriel asked whose protection, and nobody answered.

chapters.title: A Voice on the Old Frequency
chapters.text: The call came at two in the morning on a frequency the base had stopped publishing years before. Sofia knew the voice before the name: Abel Quintana, who had carried the petition through the hangar and resigned the year Mateo was promoted. He flew an old twin for whoever would hire him now, he said, and his forecast had failed; was there weather on the plateau? Mateo was in the operations room finishing a roster and had not heard Abel's voice since the clipboard. A standing order closed the base frequency to civilians and required every contact on it to be logged by name, and names from the petition still interested the security office. Abel did not ask to be left out. He only waited, his engine droning behind him, for the weather.

options.label: Give him the weather and log the call in full.
options.reply: Abel thanks them and turns away from the storm; by breakfast the security office has his name, and the names of everyone who answered him.

options.label: Give him the weather and leave the log blank.
options.reply: Abel's engine fades toward the storm's edge; Sofia's log shows a quiet night, and her carbon shows a pencilled time.

options.label: Log the call and give him nothing.
options.reply: Mateo reads the standing order into the microphone; Abel says he understands, and Sofia does not speak to Mateo until the shift ends.

callback.text: Mateo once read the commander's sentences to the cadets without changing a word. Some of those cadets now sit at radios, learning what a flight lead does when an order and a voice disagree.

condition_variants.text: The call came at two in the morning on a frequency the base had stopped publishing years before. Sofia knew the voice before the name: Abel Quintana, who had carried the petition through the hangar and resigned the year Mateo was promoted. He was flying an ambulance out of the hill towns now, for the other side, with two wounded aboard and a storm line somewhere between him and the only surgeon in reach. He wanted the plateau weather. Giving it was forbidden, and logging the call would put his name, his route and his passengers in the security office by breakfast. Mateo stood behind Sofia's chair with his roster still in his hand. Abel asked for nothing else. He only waited, engine droning behind him, for an answer from either hand.

chapters.title: Tags in Two Colors
chapters.text: After the business of the valve, Gabriel began tagging spares in two colors: white for anything that came from a depot with papers, red for whatever Bernal brought up the hill road in his lorry. Bernal bought from scrapyards, auctions and quartermasters who needed money, and he never asked what a part was for. Now an order required a full inventory of spares, with a column headed source. The white tags would fill a page. The red ones would fill three, and without them half the aircraft on the plateau would be ornaments by the end of the year. Gabriel stood in the cage beneath his receipt spike. Sofia had the inventory form. Mateo had signed for those aircraft. Noemi picked up a red-tagged gauge and asked, mildly, which of them had ever asked Bernal where anything came from.

options.label: Keep the red tags flying and list only the white.
options.reply: Gabriel hangs the red-tagged spares behind the white, and Sofia types a one-page inventory that keeps the aircraft and the secret together.

options.label: Fill the source column, red tags and all.
options.reply: The inventory runs to four pages with Bernal's name on every one; by the year's end the plateau has fewer aircraft and nothing to hide.

callback.text: Gabriel lost Orozco when he told an inspector the truth about a copied valve. He reminds them, without bitterness, that honest lists cost suppliers before they cost anyone else.

condition_variants.text: The war across the line had made Gabriel's habits dangerous. Since the business of the valve he had tagged spares in two colors: white for depot stock with papers, red for whatever Bernal brought up the hill road in his lorry. Bernal crossed the line twice a month and bought from anyone. Three red-tagged pumps still showed the other side's depot stamps under fresh paint, and Bernal sold the other side whatever he bought here. Now Alendal ordered a full inventory of spares with a column headed source, and named trade across the line a crime. Without the red tags half the plateau's aircraft would be ornaments by the end of the year. Gabriel stood in the cage beneath his receipt spike. Sofia had the form. Noemi turned a stamped pump over and said it had probably come from her mother's district.

chapters.title: A Crate through the Wire
chapters.text: The first crate of oranges in four years came up the hill road in the back of Bernal's lorry, wrapped in sacking, with Noemi's name painted on the slats in a hand that shook more than it used to. Every parcel was opened at the gate now. The corporal lifted out the fruit and found a letter underneath. Noemi read it standing in the guard hut. Her mother was ill and wanted to see her. Ruben was well and working as a mechanic for people her mother did not name, which told Noemi exactly who they were. The corporal's orders were to send letters from the hill districts to the security office. Gabriel said the lorry was going round to the stores gate anyway. Mateo, who had come down to sign for fuel, found that he was holding an orange.

options.label: Send the letter to security and log the crate.
options.reply: The security office keeps the letter a week and returns a photocopy; Noemi learns that honesty can feel exactly like being searched.

options.label: Let Gabriel take the crate round to the stores gate.
options.reply: Noemi reads the letter again in the stores cage and burns it in Gabriel's stove; the four now share her mother's handwriting.

callback.text: Years ago Sofia filed an honest permit for the first crate, and the oranges spoiled waiting for it. Noemi remembers the smell, and that the form had told the truth.

condition_variants.text: The first crate of oranges since the war began came across the line in the back of Bernal's lorry, under sacking, with Noemi's name painted on the slats in a hand that shook more than it used to. Every parcel was opened at the gate now. The corporal lifted out the fruit and found a letter underneath. Noemi read it in the guard hut. Her mother was ill and wanted to see her before the line moved again. Ruben was alive, and kept aircraft flying for the other side in a hangar less than an hour's flight away. The corporal's orders were to send any letter from across the line to the security office, unread by anyone else. Gabriel said the lorry was going round to the stores gate anyway. Mateo, who had come down to sign for fuel, found that he was holding an orange.

chapters.title: Notes in Mateo's Hand
chapters.text: The old commander was retiring, and his last order was that the security office's files from the plateau go to Alendal by summer. Sofia told Mateo on the barracks roof at dusk, while Noemi and Gabriel were still on the ladder with supper. Since the register, Mateo had written a monthly note on his wingman for the security office: short, dull, harmless, nothing Noemi had not said aloud at supper. Sofia had typed every one, with a carbon. The originals were going to Alendal. The carbons were on the slat shelf. Mateo had told himself for ten years that writing the notes was how he kept anyone worse from writing them. Noemi reached the top of the ladder, handed him a plate, and asked why the two of them looked as if the horn had just read out their names.

options.label: Tell Noemi about the notes now, all of them.
options.reply: Noemi reads the carbons by torchlight while supper goes cold; she does not shout, and she does not sit beside Mateo again that night.

options.label: Burn the carbons and let the originals go.
options.reply: Sofia feeds ten years of carbons into Gabriel's stove; Noemi is spared, and Mateo learns that relief can feel exactly like shame.

options.label: Let Sofia decide what Noemi should see.
options.reply: Sofia hands Noemi the folder and climbs down the ladder; what Noemi learns is true, but she learns it from the person who typed it.

callback.text: Noemi gave her whole family to the register because Mateo urged it. She has never asked what else the register started, and he has never offered.

The originals would be read by strangers deciding who had done what; the carbons were on the slat shelf. Mateo had told himself for ten years that writing them kept anyone worse from writing them. Noemi reached the roof and asked why they both looked guilty.

The war across the line was in its eleventh spring, and nobody on the plateau believed the radio's dates for its end any longer. The old commander was retiring. Sofia told Mateo on the barracks roof at dusk, while Noemi and Gabriel were still on the ladder with supper. Noemi reached the roof and asked why they both looked guilty.

chapters.title: A Pass for the Hill Road
chapters.text: Noemi asked for ten days' leave to see her mother, who had been ill for years and had stopped pretending otherwise in her letters. The leave form had grown since 1991. It now wanted the purpose of travel, the persons to be visited and their occupations, and a signature from the applicant's flight lead. Sofia rolled it into her machine with a carbon behind it and waited for Noemi to dictate. Ruben would be at the house, and his occupation was the kind that made a form travel further than its owner. Mateo sat on the corner of the desk with his pen out. Signing was his right, and it had never before felt so much like his decision. Gabriel came in with the fuel returns and stayed by the door.

options.label: Write every person she will see, and why.
options.reply: Sofia types the whole truth into the form; the leave waits on an office in Alendal, and Noemi waits without complaining, which is worse.

options.label: Write her mother's name and nothing more.
options.reply: Mateo signs a form with one name on it; Noemi goes to her mother, or as near as the road allows, and the four carry the rest.

callback.text: Noemi has not mentioned the notes since the night on the roof. She watches Mateo's pen now as if it might begin another one.

condition_variants.text: The war across the line was over, however the radio chose to describe its ending, and the hill road was open to anyone with a pass. The new pass form wanted the purpose of travel, the persons to be visited, and whether any of them had served the other side, for the offices that were sorting out the war's accounts. Sofia rolled it into her machine with a carbon behind it. Ruben would be at the house; he had kept the other side's aircraft flying for ten years. Mateo sat on the corner of the desk with his pen out, because the form needed a flight lead's signature, and it had never felt so much like his decision. Gabriel came in with the fuel returns and stayed by the door.

Noemi asked for ten days' leave to the river town nearest the crossing and did not say what she meant to do there; everyone in the operations room could guess. Bernal's lorry crossed twice a month. The leave form wanted the purpose of travel, the persons to be visited and a flight lead's signature. Sofia rolled it into her machine with a carbon behind it. If the form said crossing, the leave would be refused and Noemi watched. If it said rest, it would be granted, and Mateo's name would sit beneath a lie about a woman going to see her mother. Gabriel came in with the fuel returns and stayed by the door.

chapters.title: The Spike above the Bench
chapters.text: The new commander arrived in February with a pressed uniform and a habit of standing in doorways until people stood up. In March he stood in the doorway of the stores cage. Alendal, he said, meant to buy parts it could not buy openly, and he had heard that the plateau kept its aircraft flying from sources no depot listed. He looked at the steel spike above Gabriel's bench, thirty years thick with receipts: Orozco, Bernal, scrapyards, quartermasters who had needed money. He wanted every name by Friday. Gabriel said most of them were small people who had done him favors. The commander said the country was about to do them a larger one. Sofia had a blank sheet ready. Mateo, as senior flight lead, would countersign. Noemi asked what happened to a small person who said no.

options.label: Give the commander every name on the spike.
options.reply: Gabriel unhooks thirty years of receipts and hands them over; by summer Bernal is driving for Alendal, and he no longer waves at the gate.

options.label: Tell him the spike holds only old receipts.
options.reply: The commander believes Gabriel, or decides to; the names stay on the wall, and the four begin lying to a man who has not yet lied to them.

options.label: Give him the trades, but not the people.
options.reply: Gabriel writes what can be bought and roughly where, with no names attached; the commander calls it a beginning, and Sofia files it as one.

callback.text: Gabriel once kept the red tags out of an inventory. Half the names on the spike have been protected by a lie of his before, and he knows it.

Bernal's was on half the receipts, and Bernal's lorry still crossed the line twice a month; a name on the commander's list would follow him to the other side. Sofia had a blank sheet ready. The war across the line was over, and by spring the speeches had turned north. The new commander arrived in February with a pressed uniform and a phrase he used often: years of exploitation, which in his view the north had never answered for and Leasath would no longer excuse. In March he stood in the doorway of the stores cage. Alendal meant to buy parts it could not buy openly, he said, and he looked at the steel spike above Gabriel's bench, thirty years thick with receipts. He wanted every name by Friday. Mateo recognized one of the commander's sentences; he had copied it into his notebook in 1992. Sofia had a blank sheet ready. Gabriel said most of the names were small people who had done him favors. Noemi asked what happened to a small person who said no.

chapters.title: A Sentence beneath the Form
chapters.text: Visiting day fell on the morning the new commander's statements arrived, so Mateo collected signatures with half the base's families watching through the wire. The printed sheet asked each flying officer to declare readiness to carry out any order of the state without reservation. Most signed against the guard hut wall and went back to their children. Noemi read hers twice, then wrote a sentence of her own beneath the printed text, small and level: I will fly where I am ordered, and I will not say I chose it. Gabriel, who had not been asked to sign anything, watched from the stores gate. Sofia needed the sheets by noon. Mateo held Noemi's statement and his own, and understood that the commander would read the two together.

options.label: Hand in both statements exactly as written.
options.reply: Sofia files Noemi's sentence with the rest; by evening the commander has asked Mateo whether his wingman can be relied upon.

options.label: Ask Noemi to sign a clean sheet instead.
options.reply: Noemi signs the clean sheet without a word and tears up the first; the four are safe, and her sentence survives only in their memory.

options.label: Write my own sentence beneath hers.
options.reply: Mateo writes that he will obey and will remember who gave the order; the commander reads both sheets and moves them to a separate pile.

callback.text: Mateo once left the commander's sentences out of a speech to the cadets. He remembers how quiet the room became, and that he survived it.

condition_variants.text: The horn on the hangar pole carried the news from Alendal at seven in the morning, while families were already gathering at the wire for visiting day. Leasath was at war with Aurelia. The voice said years of exploitation had exhausted the country's patience, and the people at the wire listened with the faces of people adding up sons. By nine the plateau had orders to send aircraft and a ground party north, and the new commander's statements had arrived: each flying officer to declare readiness to carry out any order without reservation. Noemi read hers twice, then wrote beneath the printed text: I will fly where I am ordered, and I will not say I chose it. Gabriel watched from the stores gate. Sofia needed the sheets by noon. Mateo held Noemi's statement and his own together.

For a week the horn had been warmed up each morning for an announcement, and each morning it read the weather. Then Alendal withheld the declaration. The radio called it patience. The new commander called it nothing at all and sent his statements round regardless: each flying officer to declare readiness to carry out any order of the state without reservation. It was visiting day, and the families at the wire were laughing more than usual. Noemi read her statement twice, then wrote a sentence beneath the printed text: I will fly where I am ordered, and I will not say I chose it. Gabriel, who had been asked to sign nothing, watched from the stores gate. Sofia needed the sheets by noon. Mateo held Noemi's statement and his own, and knew they would be read together.

The war the speeches had begun promising against the north could not start while the country was still fighting itself, and the line across the hill country had not moved since spring. The new commander sent his statements of readiness round regardless: each flying officer to declare readiness to carry out any order of the state without reservation, in whichever direction it pointed. It was visiting day, and half the families at the wire had somebody on the other side. Noemi read her statement twice, then wrote a sentence beneath the printed text: I will fly where I am ordered, and I will not say I chose it. Gabriel watched from the stores gate. Sofia needed the sheets by noon. Mateo held Noemi's statement and his own and knew the commander would read them together.

chapters.title: Lights Coming On
chapters.text: Ortega, Gabriel's best apprentice, twenty-two, rolled the fuel bowser into the drainage ditch at four in the morning, at the end of a twenty-hour alert the new commander had ordered to show Alendal what the plateau could do. He was bruised, unhurt and too ashamed to eat. The commander wanted the report to say mechanical failure: a weak brake line, nobody's fault, nothing to do with alerts. Gabriel had found the brake line sound. Sofia had the duty sheet showing Ortega's hours. At dusk the four sat on the barracks roof while the plateau's lights came on one by one beneath them, the bowser still tilted in the ditch. Gabriel had trained the boy and signed his hours himself. Noemi said Ortega would want to know whether the report blamed him, the brake or the clock.
chapters.capitulated_text: The country's capitulation reached the plateau as a telephone call nobody wanted to answer, and then as three days of silence from Alendal. The horn on the hangar pole had nothing left to read. Ortega, Gabriel's best apprentice, twenty-two, had gone north with a ground party before the call came, and nothing had been heard from the party since. Whoever now received the base's reports would want them, the new commander said, in a form that blamed nobody still in the room; he suggested delayed in transit. Sofia had the true sheet: departure, last call, nothing after. At dusk the four sat on the barracks roof as the lights came on below them, fewer than before. Gabriel had trained the boy and signed his transfer. Noemi said Ortega's mother would not care who read the report, only which word was true.

options.label: Write exactly what the sheet shows.
options.reply: Sofia types the hours, the facts and the gaps; the commander signs with his jaw set, and Ortega's family receives words they can trust.

options.label: Write the commander's phrase and tell the truth in person.
options.reply: The report says what the commander wanted; Gabriel tells the rest to the people who love Ortega, at their own table, where no file will follow.

callback.text: Mateo once had his own arrival retyped to the real hour and took a commander's sarcasm for it. It is still the cheapest true sentence he has ever paid for.

condition_variants.text: The radio admitted on Tuesday what the base had been hearing for a week on other frequencies: Aurelian forces were back in Griswall. The horn on the hangar pole played the same speeches as before, a little quieter. Ortega, Gabriel's best apprentice, twenty-two, had gone north with the ground party to keep the plateau's aircraft serviceable at a borrowed field, and the party's lorry had not reported in four days. The commander wanted the report to read delayed in transit. Sofia had the true sheet: departure, last call, nothing since. At dusk the four sat on the barracks roof while the lights came on. Gabriel had trained the boy and signed his transfer, because keeping aircraft flying was what he did, and he had never once asked where these were going. Noemi said Ortega's mother would want to know which word was true.

The hangar cheered, and the cheering stopped sooner than it did in the speeches; people on the plateau had sons in uniform, and a few had cousins in the north who had married there. The commander wanted the report to read delayed in transit, because, he said, a week like this was not the week for a missing name. Sofia had the true sheet. At dusk the four sat on the barracks roof. Gabriel had trained the boy and signed his transfer, and had never once asked where these aircraft were going. The war with Aurelia had gone on for weeks, and the horn on the hangar pole had stopped playing music between the dispatches. Ortega, Gabriel's best apprentice, twenty-two, had gone north with the ground party to keep the plateau's aircraft serviceable at a borrowed field, and the party's lorry had not reported in four days. The commander wanted the report to read delayed in transit; missing, he said, was a word that frightened families and helped nobody. Sofia had the true sheet: departure, last call, nothing since. At dusk the four sat on the barracks roof while the plateau's lights came on beneath them. Gabriel had trained the boy and signed his transfer, because keeping aircraft flying was what he did, and he had never once asked where these were going. Noemi said Ortega's mother would want to know which word was true.

chapters.title: The Carbons on the Slat Shelf
chapters.text: The records officer from Alendal arrived in the last week of the year with a lorry and a list. Every base was to send its files to the archive, and the plateau's were to include everything in the operations office. The new commander told Sofia that meant top copies. Sofia's top copies said what commanders had wanted said for thirty years. The carbons on the slat shelf said the same things, with pencil wherever the top copy had been told what to say: an hour, a count of blankets, a valve, a register, a leave form, Ortega's sheet. That afternoon Gabriel had taken the horn down from the hangar pole because its wiring had finally failed, and nobody asked him to put it back. At dusk the four carried the boxes up to the barracks roof. Mateo brought his notebook. The lorry would leave at seven.
chapters.capitulated_text: The country had capitulated, and by the last week of the year the people asking for the plateau's records answered to an authority none of the four had chosen. A records officer came with a lorry and a list: every file, to be read by whoever was now deciding what Leasath's orders had been and who had given them. The new commander told Sofia that meant top copies, and that top copies were already more than enough. The carbons on the slat shelf said what had happened, with pencil wherever the top copy had been told what to say. Gabriel had taken the horn down from the hangar pole, and nobody asked him to put it back. At dusk the four carried the boxes up to the barracks roof. Mateo brought his notebook. The lorry would leave at seven.

options.label: Give the officer the carbons with the top copies.
options.reply: The lorry leaves with two boxes instead of one; whatever is read about the plateau will include the four of them, pencil and all.

options.label: Give the top copies and keep the carbons ours.
options.reply: The lorry leaves with a tidy box; the carbons go back on the slat shelf, where the four can read them to one another and to nobody else.

callback.text: Ten years of notes went into Gabriel's stove once. The slat shelf still has a gap where they stood, and all four of them know its exact width.

condition_variants.text: The ceasefire had been signed, and the plateau heard it from the radio a little before the horn, which had begun to lag behind events. By the last week of the year a records officer had come from an inquiry office in Alendal with a lorry and a list: every base's records of the war months, to establish what had been ordered and by whom. The new commander told Sofia that meant top copies. The carbons on the slat shelf said what had happened, with pencil wherever the top copy had been told what to say: an evaluation, a register, a leave form, Ortega's sheet. Gabriel had taken the horn down from the hangar pole that afternoon, and nobody asked him to put it back. At dusk the four carried the boxes up to the barracks roof. Mateo brought his notebook. The lorry would leave at seven.

The radio said, between two pieces of music, that the commander in Alendal had been removed, and for a day nobody on the plateau knew whose signature the next order would carry. Orders already in the office had been given by one hand and would now be judged by another. By the last week of the year a records officer arrived with a lorry and a list: every file from the war months, to be read by whoever was now doing the asking. The base's own commander told Sofia that meant top copies. The carbons on the slat shelf said what had happened, with pencil wherever the top copy had been told what to say. Gabriel had taken the horn down from the hangar pole, and nobody asked him to put it back. At dusk the four carried the boxes up to the barracks roof. Mateo brought his notebook.

The war with Aurelia had outlived every date the horn had given for it, and the year was ending anyway. The new commander told Sofia that meant top copies. The carbons on the slat shelf said what had happened, with pencil wherever the top copy had been told what to say: an evaluation, a register, a leave form, Ortega's sheet. Mateo brought his notebook.

condition_variants.text: The war the speeches had promised all year had not come, whether because Alendal withheld it or because the country was still fighting itself, and the plateau had spent the autumn waiting for an order that never arrived. In the last week of the year a records officer came from Alendal with a lorry and a list. The new commander told Sofia that meant top copies. The carbons on the slat shelf said the same things, with pencil wherever the top copy had been told what to say. Gabriel had taken the horn down from the hangar pole that afternoon, and nobody asked him to put it back. At dusk the four carried the boxes up to the barracks roof. Mateo brought his notebook. Noemi said a war that does not happen leaves very few files, and that this was the best thing she had heard about any year.

endings.title: One Account in Two Hands
endings.text: Whatever the records lorry carried away, nothing about the plateau is hidden among the four themselves. Mateo has stopped copying sentences from the horn. On the last page of his notebook he has written one of his own, shorter than any speech, and he lets Noemi read it before he decides whether it is true. Noemi still answers officers drily. She has seen every page with her name on it and has decided for herself which ones to forgive. Gabriel applies his oldest rule to people now: the book that belongs to a thing should tell the truth about it. Sofia teaches the new clerk to keep a carbon and to pencil nothing in it she would be ashamed to say aloud. They have been loyal and honest in turns, and have learned that the turns can be shared. None of them claims to know, in one sentence, whether the country was right. They claim only the account they gave together.

endings.title: The Top Copy
endings.text: The plateau's official account is clean, consistent and signed, and nobody outside the four will ever find it wrong in a way that can be proved. The account that matters stays where it has always been, among the four of them on the barracks roof. Mateo still carries his notebook; he has crossed out several sentences and written nothing in their place. Noemi flies, jokes, sees her mother when the road allows, and does not ask what the others still know about her; they love her too much to tell her. Gabriel's tags are tidy, and his receipt spike holds names he means to take to his grave. Sofia types beautifully for a commander who praises her clarity. They are still four friends who would stand at a gate for one another without being asked. What they cannot do is hand anyone else the account that would let a stranger understand them. They have kept each other, and the truth, in separate rooms.

endings.title: The Shelf Taken Apart
endings.text: No single betrayal explains it. Gabriel takes the slat shelf apart because nobody can say whose it is, and the four divide what is left: Mateo his notebook, Gabriel his receipt spike, Sofia a box of unused carbon paper, and Noemi the one slat that still shows her name in her mother's paint. All four are alive and working. Mateo accepts a posting in Alendal, where his notebook is admired by people who never ask where its sentences came from. Noemi leaves the service to be nearer her mother and flies crop sprayers for whoever will hire her, a phrase she took from Gabriel without asking. Gabriel stays with the aircraft, which have no opinions about one another's honesty. Sofia trains clerks elsewhere and tells them to keep carbons, without saying why. Each of the four told the truth at some cost and kept a silence at some other, and the costs never landed on the same day. When they write, they write kindly. They do not write about the plateau.
